title: Advanced Grammar Structures
description: Master the most complex and nuanced grammatical structures in English, including mixed conditionals, the subjunctive mood, advanced passive constructions, inversion, cleft sentences, and ellipsis. This course is designed for learners who have completed B1 and want to achieve grammatical precision and sophistication in both speaking and writing.

lessons.title: Second Conditional: Hypothetical Present and Future

content.content: {"time":1700000001000,"blocks":[{"id":"aB1cD2eF3g","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The second conditional is used to describe hypothetical or unreal situations in the present or future. The structure is: If + past simple, would + infinitive."}},{"id":"hI4jK5lM6n","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Unlike the first conditional, which describes realistic possibilities, the second conditional signals that the speaker considers the situation unlikely or impossible. For example: If I were the president, I would reform the tax system. — The speaker is not the president and does not expect to be."}},{"id":"oP7qR8sT9u","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Notice the use of were (not was) for all persons in formal and written English, especially in the phrase If I were you... This is a remnant of the subjunctive mood. While was is commonly accepted in informal speech, were remains standard in academic and professional writing."}},{"id":"vW0xY1zA2b","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Modal variations are also possible: If she had more time, she could learn a new language. Here, could replaces would to suggest ability rather than simple outcome. Similarly, might introduces a sense of possibility rather than certainty."}},{"id":"cD3eF4gH5i","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Common uses include giving advice (If I were you, I would apologise), making polite requests (It would be helpful if you could review the document), and expressing wishes or regrets about the present."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: If the government [invested] more in renewable energy, carbon emissions [would decrease] significantly. If I [were] in your position, I would reconsider the offer. She [could achieve] more if she [managed] her time better.
If I were you, I would reconsider the offer.

content.content: {"time":1700000002000,"blocks":[{"id":"jK6lM7nO8p","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The third conditional is used to speculate about how things could have been different in the past. The structure is: If + past perfect, would have + past participle."}},{"id":"qR9sT0uV1w","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"This structure is particularly important for expressing regret, criticism, and counterfactual reasoning. For instance: If she had submitted the report on time, the client would not have cancelled the contract. Both the condition and the result are now impossible — the deadline has passed."}},{"id":"xY2zA3bC4d","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"As with the second conditional, could have and might have can replace would have: If he had trained harder, he might have won the competition. This signals that winning was possible but not certain even in the hypothetical scenario."}},{"id":"eF5gH6iJ7k","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"A contracted form is very common in spoken English: If she'd known, she wouldn't have agreed. Note the contraction she'd for she had and wouldn't have for would not have."}},{"id":"lM8nO9pQ0r","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Third conditionals are widely used in business post-mortems (If we had researched the market properly, we would have avoided this loss), historical analysis, and literary criticism."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000003000,"blocks":[{"id":"sT1uV2wX3y","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Mixed conditionals combine elements of different conditional types to express complex relationships between past causes and present results, or present states and past consequences. They are a hallmark of advanced English proficiency."}},{"id":"zA4bC5dE6f","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Type 1 (Past condition → Present result): If + past perfect, would + infinitive. Example: If she had studied medicine, she would be a doctor now. The condition is in the past (she didn't study medicine); the result is a present situation (she is not a doctor)."}},{"id":"gH7iJ8kL9m","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Type 2 (Present condition → Past result): If + past simple, would have + past participle. Example: If he were more organised, he would have finished the project on time. The condition refers to a permanent present trait; the result refers to a specific past event."}},{"id":"nO0pQ1rS2t","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Key signal: mixed conditionals always involve a mismatch of time frames between the if-clause and the main clause. When reviewing your writing, check whether the time frame in the if-clause truly differs from the time frame in the result clause."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000004000,"blocks":[{"id":"uV3wX4yZ5a","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The subjunctive mood is used in English to express wishes, recommendations, demands, hypothetical situations, and formal suggestions. Although it has largely disappeared from everyday speech, it remains essential in academic, legal, and formal written English."}},{"id":"bC6dE7fG8h","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The present subjunctive uses the base form of the verb (without -s in the third person singular). It is triggered by verbs and expressions of demand, suggestion, recommendation, and necessity: suggest, recommend, demand, insist, require, propose, ask."}},{"id":"iJ9kL0mN1o","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Examples: The committee recommends that every applicant submit a portfolio. (not submits) | It is essential that the report be completed by Friday. (not is)"}},{"id":"pQ2rS3tU4v","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The past subjunctive (were) appears in hypothetical and wish constructions: I wish I were able to attend. | She acts as though she were in charge."}},{"id":"wX5yZ6aB7c","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The subjunctive is also required after certain fixed expressions: if need be, as it were, come what may, suffice it to say, be that as it may. Recognising these phrases and using them appropriately marks a high level of English proficiency."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000005000,"blocks":[{"id":"dE8fG9hI0j","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"While most learners are familiar with the simple passive (The letter was written), advanced English requires mastery of passive constructions across all tenses and in combination with modal and perfect aspects."}},{"id":"kL1mN2oP3q","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Perfect passive: The contract has been signed. / The building had been demolished before the planning inquiry began."}},{"id":"rS4tU5vW6x","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Modal passive: This issue must be addressed immediately. / The proposal should have been submitted last week. / The results might be announced tomorrow."}},{"id":"yZ7aB8cD9e","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Passive infinitive: The prisoner is believed to have escaped. / The results are expected to be published next month."}},{"id":"fG0hI1jK2l","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Causative passive (have/get something done): We are having the office renovated. / She had her car serviced yesterday. This structure is used when a subject arranges for someone else to perform an action on their behalf."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000006000,"blocks":[{"id":"mN3oP4qR5s","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Inversion refers to reversing the normal subject-verb word order for emphasis, formality, or stylistic effect. It is common in written and formal spoken English, in literary texts, and in negative and conditional structures."}},{"id":"tU6vW7xY8z","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Negative adverbial inversion: When a sentence begins with a negative or restrictive adverb, the auxiliary verb comes before the subject. Common triggers: Never, Seldom, Rarely, Not only, Not until, No sooner, Hardly, Scarcely, Little, Only then."}},{"id":"aB9cD0eF1g","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Examples: Never before had the committee faced such a crisis. | Not only did she pass the exam, but she also achieved the highest score. | Hardly had we arrived when the storm began."}},{"id":"hI2jK3lM4n","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Conditional inversion (formal alternative to if-clauses): In formal writing, if may be omitted and the auxiliary inverted instead. Should you require further assistance, please contact us. | Had the report been submitted on time, the project would have proceeded."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000007000,"blocks":[{"id":"oP5qR6sT7u","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Cleft sentences are used to give special emphasis to one part of a sentence by splitting it into two clauses. They are especially common in formal written English and in emphatic speech."}},{"id":"vW8xY9zA0b","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"It-cleft: The structure is It is/was + emphasised element + relative clause. Example: It was the CEO who made the final decision. (emphasis on the CEO) | It is the lack of funding that prevents progress. (emphasis on the cause)"}},{"id":"cD1eF2gH3i","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Wh-cleft (pseudo-cleft): The structure begins with a what-clause followed by be. Example: What we need is a comprehensive strategy. | What surprised everyone was his sudden resignation."}},{"id":"jK4lM5nO6p","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"All-cleft: Uses all to restrict or narrow focus: All I want is a clear explanation. | All she did was smile."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000008000,"blocks":[{"id":"qR7sT8uV9w","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Ellipsis is the omission of words that are understood from context. It is used to avoid repetition and create more natural, fluent language. Mastering ellipsis is essential for achieving a natural, advanced register in both speaking and writing."}},{"id":"xY0zA1bC2d","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Verb phrase ellipsis: The repeated verb phrase is omitted. She can speak French, and he can too. (= he can speak French too) | I've finished my report. Have you? (= Have you finished yours?)"}},{"id":"eF3gH4iJ5k","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Auxiliary ellipsis: Only the auxiliary verb is retained. She hasn't been sleeping well, but he has. | They were expecting a refund and so were we."}},{"id":"lM6nO7pQ8r","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Substitution is closely related: instead of omitting words, a substitute word (so, do, one, ones, the same) is used. Do you think the proposal will succeed? I think so."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000009000,"blocks":[{"id":"sT9uV0wX1y","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Advanced reported speech goes far beyond he said that. Sophisticated writers use a wide variety of reporting verbs that encode the speaker's attitude, intention, or the illocutionary force of the original utterance."}},{"id":"zA2bC3dE4f","type":"header","data":{"text":"Categories of reporting verbs:","level":3}},{"id":"gH5iJ6kL7m","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Saying/telling: state, maintain, assert, claim, declare, announce, remark","Suggesting/advising: suggest, recommend, propose, advise, urge, encourage","Promising/threatening: promise, guarantee, threaten, warn, vow","Accusing/admitting: accuse (of), admit, deny, confess, acknowledge, insist"]}},{"id":"nO8pQ9rS0t","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Tense backshift is standard when reporting past speech: present → past, past simple → past perfect, will → would. However, backshift is not required when the reported statement is still true at the time of reporting: He said that London is the capital of England."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

lessons.title: Putting It All Together: Advanced Grammar in Context

content.content: {"time":1700000010000,"blocks":[{"id":"uV1wX2yZ3a","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"In authentic B2+ writing and speech, advanced grammar structures rarely appear in isolation. A single paragraph in an academic essay or a formal report may employ inversion for emphasis, a cleft sentence to highlight a key argument, the subjunctive in a recommendation, and ellipsis to avoid repetition — all working together to produce a polished, coherent text."}},{"id":"bC4dE5fG6h","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Consider the following passage: It is the failure to invest in education that has led to the current skills gap. Were governments to allocate adequate resources, the situation might have been prevented. What is needed now is not incremental reform, but a fundamental rethinking of the curriculum. Seldom has there been greater consensus among educators, yet little has been done."}},{"id":"iJ7kL8mN9o","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"In this passage: an it-cleft opens the argument; a mixed conditional with inversion speculates about the past; a wh-cleft emphasises the prescription; and negative adverbial inversion (Seldom has there been) closes with rhetorical force."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}
